sources.title: Teachers Warn That Students Are Losing the Ability to Think as They Lean on AI for Everything
sources.notes: The article frames AI-assisted writing as a possible threat to thinking and cites an MIT essay-writing study plus a New York Times essay containing expert commentary. Its headline and synthesis are not admitted as scientific findings.

sources.title: Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt when Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing Task

design.assignment: participants randomly assigned across three groups, balanced with respect to age and gender according to available full-text mirrors

observations_admitted: The three experimental conditions showed different EEG connectivity patterns during the essay-writing task.
The LLM condition showed weaker reported connectivity than Search Engine and Brain-only conditions in the study's analyses.
LLM-condition participants had lower reported ownership and greater difficulty accurately quoting their own essays.
In session 4, the LLM-to-Brain subgroup showed reduced alpha and beta connectivity relative to the study's comparison framing.
claims_not_admitted: LLMs cause durable cognitive decline across tasks
lower EEG connectivity proves loss of intelligence
the experiment establishes long-term population-level impairment
limitations_preserved: The study is context-dependent and centered on essay writing in an educational setting.
The authors state that results cannot be directly generalized to other LLMs.
The task was not decomposed into subtasks such as idea generation and drafting.
The reported EEG analysis focused on connectivity patterns rather than spectral power changes.
The institutional project page identifies larger and more diverse samples and longitudinal work as future research needs.
A later methodological comment raises reproducibility, EEG-method, reporting, transparency, and sample-size concerns.

sources.title: New York Times essay on student writing and AI
sources.notes: Futurism attributes expert commentary from Ronald T. Kellogg and Steve Graham to this essay. The linked page was not directly reviewable in the current retrieval path, so expert statements are not promoted as primary empirical findings.

sources.title: Comment on: Your Brain on ChatGPT: Accumulation of Cognitive Debt When Using an AI Assistant for Essay Writing Tasks
Scaffolding human and AI instruction: Neural alignment and learning gains in online education
observations_admitted: Both human- and AI-led structured pre-lecture interactions were associated with improved learning and greater neural alignment compared with no interaction in the authors' overall framing.
The AI-interaction group was statistically comparable to the human-interaction group on reported learning outcomes.
No significant effects were observed for recall or transfer scores between human- and AI-interaction groups in the reported comparison.
The AI group reported lower social closeness and showed lower gaze alignment than the human group on some measures.

sources.title: Your brain on ChatGPT, but whose brain? The missing adolescent in AI-cognition research
observations_admitted: The paper explicitly distinguishes cognitive debt, reduced neural engagement, and reduced neural connectivity.
It states that lower neural activity does not necessarily mean worse cognition and can reflect efficient processing in other contexts.

It characterizes its adolescent cognitive-offloading account as a hypothesis and states that direct longitudinal or experimental evidence for long-term adolescent executive-function effects is not yet available.
It frames the key design distinction as AI substituting for versus scaffolding executive-function processes.

next_source_actions: Review the full Kosmyna preprint methods/results directly and extract exact statistics rather than relying on secondary numerical summaries.
Verify whether a peer-reviewed successor/version of arXiv:2506.08872 exists.
Expand peer-reviewed scaffold/intervention studies with delayed unaided transfer outcomes.
Add null findings and studies where AI support does not change later unaided capability.
Build longitudinal evidence sufficient to distinguish temporary task-state effects from durable capability change.
